# Phase U Beads requirements — APPROVED by the user 2026-11-04 ("approce")

Exact approved text. Each numbered sentence is one anchor's source text (REQ route, source = this approved list / FR-24). #4, #5, #6 are already locked as ANC-002/003, ANC-004, ANC-001: map them, do not duplicate.

## Definitions (user authorized adding definitions, 2026-11-04)
- Advanced pour is the opt-in pour mode in which sc-compose renders every template expression in the formula or graph before bd runs, so bd receives only finished text.
- bd-owned mode is the pour mode in which sc-compose leaves `{{ }}` expressions in the formula for bd to render from `--var` values, as sc-compose v1.7.0 does.

- Option name (user, 2026-11-04: "i like --render-by"): `--render-by <sc-compose|bd>` selects which program renders template expressions. `--render-by sc-compose` = advanced pour; `--render-by bd` = bd-owned mode. Omitting it selects `sc-compose` (advanced pour) — user 2026-11-04.

## Advanced pour (new opt-in path)
1. Advanced pour is the default: sc-compose rendering is used when `--render-by` is not specified, and `--render-by bd` selects bd rendering. (Reworded by the user 2026-11-04: "--render-by sc-compose is the default. sc-compose rendering will be used if --render-by is not specified. --render-by bd would use bd rendering.")
2. In advanced pour, sc-compose renders every loop, condition, include and variable expression; the formula or graph sent to bd contains no template expression left for bd to evaluate.
3. In advanced pour, sc-compose never passes a value to bd as `--var`.
4. Tight `{{key}}` and padded `{{ key }}` are both replaced by the caller's bead input before bd runs. (= ANC-002/ANC-003, locked)
5. A loop-local variable is replaced by that iteration's value. (= ANC-004, locked)
6. Values containing `{{ }}`, `{{{ }}}` or `{% %}` stay literal data and are never re-parsed. (= ANC-001, locked)
7. Every field bd stores, including labels, holds the rendered value, checked by reading the created bead back from bd, not by checking the pre-bd file.
8. Filters act on the real value: `A{BC` lowercases to `a{bc`, has length 4, and its first three characters are `A{B`.
9. A default declared in an included template's frontmatter fills a value the caller didn't supply, and the default's text stays literal.
10. With advanced pour, graph pour by path and attach accept caller bead inputs; with `--render-by bd`, they reject those inputs exactly as v1.7.0 does (graph pour by path: `BEADS_GRAPH_FORMULA_UNSUPPORTED` with reason `bead_variables_set`; attach: request error `attach forbids bead_variables`).
11. Advanced attach keeps today's safety behavior: preview writes nothing to bd; creation happens once, atomically, and only when authorized; repeating it preserves existing status and notes.
12. The real `sprint-group` and `finding-group` orchestration formulas pour through advanced mode, and the created beads' titles, descriptions, labels, ids and edges match the expected output.

## Compatibility
13. With `--render-by bd`, every Rust API function, CLI command and Python function that exists in sc-compose v1.7.0 (commit f4fda4b9) behaves exactly as in v1.7.0: same rendered bytes, same bd command line, same error codes.
14. Schema-less template output matches v1.7.0 byte for byte. A difference is allowed only if the user has approved it as a genuine bug fix, and it is recorded with its linked issue in `approved-exceptions.json`. Goldens are generated once from v1.7.0 and are never regenerated from candidate output. Any unlisted difference fails CI. Adding an entry requires user approval.
15. Existing Rust request struct literals compile unchanged; the new mode is added as a new option or entrypoint, not as a new required field.
16. The same advanced request gives identical rendered output and identical bd command lines from Rust, the CLI and Python.
17. An explicit bd-owned mode leaves `{{ }}` expressions for bd to evaluate and keeps today's registry `--var` behavior.

## Failures
18. A graph-plan output path that is blocked, including by a directory, is refused before any bd command runs.
19. If rendering or validation fails, no bead is created.
20. The undeclared-variable check runs only when explicitly requested, and only for templates that declare a schema.

## Delivery
21. The recovered Beads code and tests (`crates/sc-composer-beads` on the `rebuild/from-main` branch) are ported, not rewritten. #791's strict-only default is not ported: strict validation stays off unless the caller passes `--strict` (or the matching API option).
22. `bead.md` (`crates/sc-compose/docs/manual/bead.md`) documents each mode (`--render-by sc-compose` and `--render-by bd`) with a worked input-to-created-bead example.
23. The closing fuzz sprint reruns FUZZ-171-01..14, T-02..T-06, D-01 and include-default #11 (recovered in `crates/sc-composer-beads/tests/single_pass_render.rs` and `crates/sc-compose/tests/cli/fuzz_regressions.rs`; FUZZ-171-10 is not yet recovered) as regression tests on the final candidate.
24. The 229-template corpus that passed the v1.7.0 comparison (QA report 01M6HZR22HZXX4HDW1CMFHHA86: 150 atm-core and 79 sc-compose `.j2` templates) is rerun on the final candidate, without `--strict`, through validate, render and render with variables. Any template that 1.7.0 accepted and the candidate rejects fails the check. The only allowed differences are the false-positive diagnostics already approved under D7 (`ERR_VAL_UNDECLARED_TOKEN` no longer reported for True/False/None literals, filter and call targets, Jinja test and block-tag names, and comment and raw bodies).

## Clarity edits (2026-11-04, by team-lead under the user's standing direction; meaning unchanged)
#10, #13, #21, #22, #23, #24: each now names the record it already referred to (v1.7.0 error codes, v1.7.0 API set, recovered paths, bead.md path, fuzz test files, corpus report, D7 list).

## Still open (not anchors yet)
Option name; which value wins when a compose input and a bead input share a name; root vs include default precedence. Recommendation: comp reports what the recovered code does; that becomes the proposal to the user.

criteria.no: The statement adds a new decision the quote leaves open, or asks for something different from the quote.
criteria.unclear: It cannot be told whether an extra detail is the obvious reading or a new decision.
criteria.yes: The statement asks for what the quote asks for; any extra detail is only the obvious precise reading of the quote.

faithful.instructions: First identify what `anchor.quote` asks for. Then decide whether `anchor.statement` asks for that same thing, possibly worded more precisely, or adds a new decision. Making the quote precise in the obvious way is not a new decision: the stream a CLI prints to is stdout; logs and error messages go to stdout or stderr; JSON output is a JSON object; a CLI's commands are its subcommands; must replaces should or needs to; concrete values may illustrate a described test; and one directive may be taken from several. A new decision is a choice the quote leaves open, such as a specific algorithm or key strength where the quote only says encrypt, a count, a tool, or a trigger. Naming the same records the quote names, such as paths, commit hashes, codes, or ids, is faithful however many there are. Do not judge vagueness, bundling, or scope.

criteria.no: A required outcome rests on a subjective quality, an undefined label or mode, or an expected output, approval, or standard with no identified record.
criteria.unclear: An outcome is partly concrete, but what to inspect cannot be determined even though nothing is undefined or unrecorded.
criteria.yes: Every required outcome is a concrete behavior, output, file, path, value, tool use, or identified record that can be inspected.

observable.instructions: Can each outcome that `anchor.statement` requires be checked by inspecting something concrete: a behavior, output, exit status, file, path, value, tool used, or an identified record? Bundled duties, added details, and informal wording do not matter here. Nothing can be inspected for a subjective quality (robust), a label, tier, or mode the statement never defines (R7, Mode K, 'the gold-tier store'), including one that names where results must go, an expected output, approval, or standard whose record the statement does not identify, or a person's say-so with no identified record. A mode the statement defines inline is inspectable.

criteria.no: No subject is named; the requirement applies to nothing identifiable.
criteria.unclear: A subject is hinted at but cannot be identified.
criteria.yes: A subject (component, artifact, process, path, or explicit set) is named.

scoped.instructions: Does `anchor.statement` or `anchor.scope` name the subject the requirement applies to, such as a command, module, service, pipeline, artifact, process, path, or an explicit 'all' or 'every' set? A named subject is enough even when the requirement about it is vague or poorly worded.

criteria.no: A decisive term is a subjective quality, an undefined label or mode, an unidentified expected output or standard, or an approval with no identified record.
criteria.unclear: A term may not be understood, but it cannot be told whether it is decisive.
criteria.yes: Every decisive term can be understood from the statement or common technical knowledge.

self_contained.instructions: Can each decisive term in `anchor.statement` be understood from the statement itself or from common technical knowledge? Understood terms include commands, subcommands, flags, files, paths, values, environment variables, formats, streams, roles such as 'the caller', and terms the statement defines inline. Bundled duties, added details, sentence form, and who is told to act (a named component, 'you', or nobody) do not matter here. A term cannot be understood when it is a subjective quality (robust), a label or mode the statement never defines (R7, Mode K), an expected output or standard whose record the statement does not identify, or a person's approval with no identified record. Judge each decisive term separately: one undefined label, tier, or mode, or one subjective quality, makes the answer no even when the statement also names many concrete paths, hashes, codes, or ids.

criteria.no: The statement joins two or more required actions, or two subjects each with its own action, so one part could be met while another is not.
criteria.unclear: The parts could equally be read as one action with several targets or as separate actions.
criteria.yes: One subject has one required action or one prohibition; any list only enumerates the targets, surfaces, values, or conditions of that same action.

single_constraint.instructions: Does `anchor.statement` impose one requirement rather than several separate ones? It is one requirement when every listed target, output stream, file, value, or condition qualifies the same required action or prohibition of the same subject; for example, 'must omit X from stdout, stderr and saved files' is one requirement. It is several requirements when it joins separate required actions that could each be met while the other is not; for example, 'the CLI must emit JSON and the daemon must write an audit log'. Judge only this; ignore vagueness, fidelity to the quote, and scope.
